params.question: Which of the following presentations would be MOST easily overlooked as PCOS if the clinician assesses only menstrual history?

answers.text: Oligomenorrhoea, acne along the jawline, and BMI 30 kg/m²

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This woman's oligomenorrhoea is a clear menstrual red flag that would prompt investigation. Her androgenic and metabolic features confirm the picture, but the menstrual irregularity alone would raise suspicion.

answers.text: Amenorrhoea of 6 months, elevated serum testosterone, and acanthosis nigricans

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Amenorrhoea is a prominent menstrual abnormality that would immediately trigger evaluation. Although her metabolic sign (acanthosis nigricans) confirms the broader picture, the menstrual history alone is clearly abnormal.

answers.text: Regular 28-day cycles, hirsutism on the upper lip, and fasting hyperinsulinaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Some women with PCOS menstruate regularly but have anovulatory cycles — this only becomes apparent when fertility is desired or when androgenic and metabolic features are actively sought. A clinician who checks only cycle regularity would miss this presentation entirely.

answers.text: Cycles every 45 days, mild hair thinning, and normal BMI

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cycles every 45 days constitute oligomenorrhoea (cycle length >35 days), which would be detected on menstrual history alone. Even with a normal BMI, the menstrual irregularity flags the need for further workup.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: PCOS presents along three overlapping domains — menstrual dysfunction, androgen excess, and metabolic disturbance. Some women have regular but anovulatory cycles, making single-domain assessment insufficient to detect all cases.

Well done. PCOS can present with regular cycles that are actually anovulatory — a clinical trap that highlights why all three domains (menstrual, androgenic, metabolic) must be assessed systematically.

interactions.label: A 25-year-old woman fulfils two positive Rotterdam criteria: oligomenorrhoea and

params.question: A 25-year-old woman fulfils two positive Rotterdam criteria: oligomenorrhoea and polycystic ovarian morphology on TVS. Her serum TSH is normal. What must be completed before confirming a diagnosis of PCOS?

answers.text: All three Rotterdam features, including hyperandrogenism, must be demonstrated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Rotterdam criteria require any two of the three features — not all three. This woman already meets the positive diagnostic threshold with oligomenorrhoea and polycystic morphology.

answers.text: Insulin resistance must be confirmed with fasting insulin or HOMA-IR

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Insulin resistance is central to the pathophysiology of PCOS but is not one of the three Rotterdam diagnostic criteria. It need not be demonstrated to make the diagnosis.

answers.text: Remaining mimics — hyperprolactinaemia, late-onset CAH, and Cushing syndrome — must be excluded

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion. Even after meeting two positive Rotterdam criteria, conditions that mimic PCOS — including hyperprolactinaemia, late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia (17-OHP), and Cushing syndrome — must be systematically excluded before the diagnosis is confirmed.

answers.text: A repeat TVS after three menstrual cycles is needed to confirm persistent polycystic morphology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A single TVS demonstrating ≥20 follicles per ovary or ovarian volume ≥10 mL satisfies the polycystic morphology criterion. There is no requirement for repeat imaging to confirm persistence.

overallFeedback.feedback: PCOS requires two of three positive Rotterdam features AND exclusion of mimics (thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, late-onset CAH, Cushing syndrome, androgen-secreting tumours). Meeting the positive criteria alone is insufficient for diagnosis.

Exactly right. PCOS uniquely requires both a positive arm (2 of 3 Rotterdam features) and a negative arm (systematic exclusion of all mimics) — a dual requirement that distinguishes it from most diagnoses.

params.question: A 27-year-old woman with PCOS and BMI 29 kg/m² presents with oligomenorrhoea and hirsutism. She has no immediate fertility plans. What is the recommended first-line intervention?

answers.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill to restore regular withdrawal bleeds

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While COCs are effective for menstrual regulation and suppression of androgen levels, they are second-line pharmacotherapy. Lifestyle modification must be tried first as it addresses the underlying metabolic dysfunction rather than masking it.

answers.text: Metformin 500 mg twice daily to reduce insulin resistance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Metformin improves insulin sensitivity and may help restore ovulatory function, but it is an adjunct to lifestyle modification, not a replacement for it. The metabolic improvement from weight loss often exceeds what metformin alone achieves.

Correct. Even a modest 5–10% weight loss reduces hyperinsulinaemia, which in turn lowers ovarian androgen synthesis and raises SHBG — directly breaking the pathophysiological cycle at its root. This significantly restores menstrual regularity in overweight women with PCOS.

answers.text: Clomiphene citrate to induce regular ovulatory cycles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Clomiphene citrate is the first-line ovulation induction agent when fertility is desired, but this patient has no immediate fertility plans. It does not address the underlying metabolic dysfunction driving her symptoms.

overallFeedback.feedback: In PCOS, lifestyle modification targeting 5–10% weight loss is always first-line regardless of the presenting concern. It reduces hyperinsulinaemia, lowers ovarian androgen production, and raises SHBG — addressing the root pathophysiology before medications are added.

Correct. Lifestyle modification is always first-line in PCOS management because even 5–10% weight loss directly breaks the insulin resistance–androgen excess cycle at its root, improving menstrual regularity, androgen levels, and metabolic parameters.
